chapter_title: The Chapter of the Nazorean who questions the Teacher
chapter_note: This chapter is dominated by hagiographic dialogue frame and moral/judicial exhortation. A clear New Testament/Gospel overlay appears in ¶10 (“the saviour has said…” with the treasure/heart saying; Mt 6 in apparatus). The remaining argument about God-as-judge is presented as situational disputation and ethical reasoning rather than systematic cosmological mechanics; no degree-structures, body↔cosmos maps, or named Manichaean cosmic hypostases appear. Thus only a small, impersonal maxim in ¶11 reads like a detachable older teaching aphorism; most other material is frame/pastoral/overlay.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic narrative setup (“Once again, it happened…”) and hagiographic scene-setting with “apostle” mark editorial frame.
Dialogue attribution (“The apostle speaks…”) and rhetorical exchange belong to the compilation’s disputation frame rather than impersonal cosmological teaching.
Question posed within the staged dialogue; “to the apostle” keeps it inside the redactional frame.
Repeated dialogue tags (“Then says the apostle…”) plus lacunose rhetorical jab; the ‘judge is my God’ thesis is delivered as a scene-line within the frame.
Continues the narrated disputation with the Nazorean’s objection; situational rhetoric rather than systematic cosmology; still anchored by ‘says to him’ in-scene voice.

paragraphs.core_text: “The judge is not a man of wickedness, but rather the work counteracts wickedness, limiting the evil. Nevertheless, what you have recounted is that the judge shall go and punish, kill and slay. He acts like this that he might annul the evil and impede the wickedness in the person; and lay it upon the head of the sinner.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the dialogue attribution (“The apostle, in turn, speaks to him:”) as compilation-frame (Layer 2). Remainder is an impersonal explanatory maxim about limiting evil via judgement.
paragraphs.temporal_note: After stripping the speaker tag, the remainder reads like a general, impersonal principle (how judgement functions to limit Evil), detachable from the narrative wrapper. Still not strongly cosmological, so the ‘core’ here is tentative and limited to the maxim-like teaching.
Imperatival exhortation (“pay attention”) and moral reassurance about not fearing judgement for those who have not sinned; ethical paraenesis without cosmological mechanics.
Moral-causal argument about Sin returning on the sinner’s head and reward for good deeds; ethical instruction register rather than systematic cosmology.
Generalized moral dualism (“obey the devil… won over to the truth and the knowledge…”) presented as exhortation; lacks cosmological hierarchy or technical mapping.

Explicit Gospel/NT entry vector: “Even as the saviour has said” with the treasure/heart saying (Mt 6 in apparatus). Regardless of suitability to Manichaean ethics, this language enters via NT citation.

paragraphs.core_text: “Nevertheless, God has not done anything that is ev[il to] them, rather they to themselves. It is their own deeds that shall con- demn them and cast them in the gehenna of burning.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Standalone, aphoristic theodicy principle (evil self-incurred; deeds condemn) with no dialogue tags. ‘Gehenna’ is Judaeo-Christian vocabulary, so the dating is uncertain; however the sentence reads like a detachable maxim not dependent on NT citation formula.

Recompense-for-deeds exhortation (“people of good deeds… recompense…”)—paraenetic and reward-focused; ‘kingdom of light’ here functions as ethical reward language rather than a mapped cosmological station.
Concluding exhortation/summary (“Behold now…”) in second-person persuasion voice; matches end-of-chapter paraenesis and the chapter’s strong pastoral drift signal.
